patterns.title: Opposite-End Two Pointers
patterns.summary: Converge left and right pointers towards the center to find pairs, partition elements, or reverse collections in linear time.
trigger_cues: Array or string is sorted (or can be sorted in O(N log N))
Target is to find a pair or triplet summing to a value
Partitioning elements or checking palindromes in-place
invariant_rules: Pointers satisfy left < right at each step
All candidate solutions outside [left, right] have already been evaluated and eliminated
If current_sum < target, incrementing left strictly increases the sum (assuming sorted non-decreasing)
common_pitfalls: Applying to an unsorted array without sorting first
Off-by-one index with right = size vs right = size - 1
Omitting pointer advance in branch causing an infinite loop

patterns.title: Dynamic Sliding Window
patterns.summary: Expand a contiguous window with a right pointer while contracting with a left pointer to satisfy a state invariant.
trigger_cues: Subarray or substring contiguous range requirement
Longest/shortest range satisfying condition (e.g., at most K distinct elements)
Running sum or character frequency within a range
invariant_rules: Window [left, right] contains elements that maintain or approach the target constraint
Right pointer expands the candidate range by 1 on each outer loop
Left pointer contracts the window until the invariant is restored
common_pitfalls: Contracting window before evaluating or updating state counters
Re-scanning window from scratch rather than updating incremental frequency diffs
Failing to clean up map keys when frequency drops to 0

patterns.title: Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd's Cycle Finding)
patterns.summary: Move two pointers at different speeds (1x and 2x) across a linked list or cyclical sequence to detect cycles or locate midpoints in O(1) space.
trigger_cues: Detect if a linked list or sequence contains a cycle
Find the midpoint of a linked list in a single pass
Find the entry node of a circular loop
invariant_rules: In a cycle of length L, the relative distance between fast and slow decreases by 1 node per iteration
Slow and fast will meet in at most L iterations once slow enters the cycle
When slow and fast meet, resetting slow to head and moving both at 1x finds the cycle entrance
common_pitfalls: Null pointer dereference: forgetting to check both fast and fast->next before accessing fast->next->next
Misidentifying midpoint for even-length lists (depending on slow/fast initialization)
Overcomplicating with auxiliary hash sets when O(1) space is achievable

patterns.title: Monotonic Stack
patterns.summary: Maintain elements in a strictly increasing or decreasing order on a stack to resolve nearest greater/smaller element queries in linear time.
trigger_cues: Find the next greater or smaller element for each index in an array
Find largest rectangle in histogram or trapping rain water bounds
Daily temperatures or span evaluations
invariant_rules: The stack always contains indices whose values satisfy the monotonic invariant (e.g. descending)
Incoming element pops all stack items that violate the invariant, resolving their queries
Each element is pushed once and popped at most once, giving amortized O(N) time
common_pitfalls: Storing values in the stack instead of indices when distances or indices are required
Using strict < versus <= leading to duplicate values improperly grouped
Assuming O(N^2) complexity because of nested while loop: each element enters and leaves once

patterns.title: State-Space Backtracking
patterns.summary: Explore state candidates recursively and systematically undo state modifications (backtrack) upon encountering invalid states.
trigger_cues: Generate all permutations, combinations, or partitions
Constrained search spaces (e.g. Sudoku, Word Search, N-Queens)
Find all valid decision paths through a graph or tree
invariant_rules: State before branching is identically restored after the recursive call returns
Base condition correctly records a completed leaf snapshot into results
Pruning condition terminates branches early if partial state cannot lead to valid solution
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to undo state modification (pop_back or reset flag), corrupting neighboring branches
Missing base return condition leading to recursion stack overflow
Failing to sort input array before handling duplicate candidates

patterns.title: Binary Search and Search-Space Halving
patterns.summary: Halve a sorted search space one comparison at a time. The technique is not the loop but the invariant: the answer, if it exists, stays inside the current window.
trigger_cues: The input is sorted, or can be sorted once and queried many times
The answer is a position or boundary, not just a boolean
A range query can be framed as finding the first index at or after a value
A sorted container exposes contiguous random access (array, not linked list)
invariant_rules: At every iteration, if the target exists, it exists inside [lo, hi)
Each branch discards only indices provably unable to hold the target
Exhausting the window (lo == hi) proves absence rather than merely failing to find it
Pick one boundary convention (half-open or closed) and use it consistently
common_pitfalls: Mixing a half-open window with a closed-window body, producing off-by-one errors that only appear at array edges
Using binary search over a linked list, which costs O(N log N) and is worse than a linear scan
Returning before checking whether the window ever emptied, so absence is reported as 'not found' without proof
Assuming the loop is O(1) because it has no inner loop, and forgetting that each probe is a memory access

patterns.title: Hash Map Frequency Counting
patterns.summary: Trade an O(N) rescan for an O(1) lookup by counting as you go. The hash table does not answer range questions, so knowing when it is the wrong tool matters as much as knowing when to use it.
trigger_cues: The question asks how many times something occurred
Pairs, anagrams, duplicates, or complements are involved
Order is irrelevant and only equality matters
The alphabet is small enough that a fixed-size table beats a hash map
invariant_rules: The count map always describes exactly the elements seen so far
Keys hash equal when they are equal, which is what makes lookup sound
Look for the complement *before* inserting the current element, or you will match an element with itself
common_pitfalls: Inserting first and querying second, which lets a single element pair with itself
Expecting sorted iteration or range queries from a hash table -- neither is supported at any price
Ignoring that the worst case is O(N) when all keys collide, which an attacker can induce deliberately
Using a hash table when the input is already sorted and range queries are needed

patterns.title: Heap as a Priority Queue
patterns.summary: When the question is 'which one comes out next' over a changing set, a heap is the structure that mirrors it. It gives O(1) peek and O(log N) insert and delete, and nothing else.
trigger_cues: The problem repeatedly asks for the smallest or largest remaining item
Dijkstra or Prim's frontier must expand by minimum key
Top-k or a running median over a stream
Several sorted sequences must be merged lazily
invariant_rules: Every parent is at or above (min-heap) its two children, and that is the only ordering guaranteed
The extreme value is always at index 0, with no search required
Push appends at the next free slot, which preserves the complete shape, then sifts up
Sift-down moves toward the *smaller* child, because moving toward the larger re-breaks the relation
common_pitfalls: Expecting the k-th smallest element in O(1) -- the heap supports only the extreme value
Building by repeated push (O(N log N)) when heapify is available (O(N))
Sift-down comparing against the larger child, which produces an invalid heap that still looks plausible
Merging two heaps directly, which costs O(N); a loser tree or balanced tree is the right structure

patterns.title: Trie and Prefix Reuse
patterns.summary: Store keys as shared prefixes rather than whole units. Prefix search then costs the same as membership, and lexicographic order falls out of traversal.
trigger_cues: Many keys share a prefix, or questions ask about prefixes
Autocomplete, spell checking, or dictionary lookup
Lexicographic iteration over a set of strings
A small fixed alphabet where a fixed child array is affordable
invariant_rules: Following a key's characters from the root reaches a node if and only if the key is present
A key is complete exactly when the final node's terminal flag is set -- a successful walk alone is not enough
Shared prefixes are stored once, so node count tracks distinct prefixes rather than total key length
common_pitfalls: Conflating 'is a prefix of some key' with 'is a key', which is the classic trie bug
Forgetting to prune on delete, leaving orphaned nodes and leaking space
Assuming membership is faster than a hash map -- it is O(L) against O(1) expected
Using fixed fan-out over a large or sparse key set and wasting most of every node's child array

patterns.title: Choosing a Graph Traversal
patterns.summary: Traversal order is a consequence of the algorithm, not of the data. The choice between BFS, DFS and Dijkstra is determined by the graph's model and by what is being asked.
trigger_cues: Reachability, or shortest path measured in edge count
Cycle detection, topological order, or connected components
Cheapest route rather than fewest hops
The graph has negative weights, or may have them
invariant_rules: Every marked-visited vertex is genuinely reachable, and every reachable vertex is visited before termination
BFS processes in non-decreasing distance because it dequeues from the front
A topological order requires a DAG; no zero-in-degree vertex remaining is the cycle certificate
Dijkstra requires non-negative weights, because that is what makes an extracted distance final
common_pitfalls: Running Dijkstra on a graph with a negative edge, which returns a wrong answer rather than a slow one
Using BFS where weighted distance is required, silently returning the fewest-hops path
Attempting a topological sort on a cyclic graph and treating the stall as a bug rather than a proof
Forgetting that a visited set is a termination guarantee, not just an optimisation

patterns.title: Dynamic Programming with Memoisation
patterns.summary: When subproblems repeat, the fix is to compute each once. The discipline is choosing a state that both suffices to determine the answer and minimises the state count.
trigger_cues: The same subproblem is reachable by many different paths
Overlapping subproblems plus a provable optimal substructure
The naive recursion is exponential but the state space looks polynomial
Counting paths, subsets, or arrangements with constraints
invariant_rules: A state is sufficient only if two calls sharing it must return the same value
Every state is computed exactly once, after all of its dependencies
The recurrence references only strictly smaller states, so the measure decreases and recursion terminates
Bottom-up and memoised top-down produce identical results, differing only in which states are visited
common_pitfalls: Memorising on a state that omits a parameter the answer depends on, silently returning wrong answers
Using DP where the subproblems do not overlap, paying a table's cost for nothing
Failing to prove optimal substructure, as with greedy interval selection
Rolling arrays without matching the iteration direction, which quietly changes which items may be reused

patterns.title: Backtracking with Sound Pruning
patterns.summary: Enumerate candidates incrementally and abandon a partial construction the moment it provably cannot lead to an answer. Pruning changes the constant in the exponent, not the exponent itself, so its soundness is a correctness property.
trigger_cues: Constraints only become checkable as the solution is built
Every valid solution is wanted, not just the first
The candidates form a tree and local choices interact
N-queens, permutations under constraints, subset selection under capacity
invariant_rules: On entry to a call, state reflects exactly the decisions in the current path
Pruning may only discard a subtree that provably contains no solution
The undo at each level must restore state exactly, or later candidates are explored from a corrupted base
Apply, recurse, undo -- in that order
common_pitfalls: Pruning a branch that did contain a solution, which returns a wrong answer indistinguishable from a correct one
Forgetting the undo, or doing it before the recursion, which corrupts state several levels later
Recomputing the same subproblem instead of memoising -- when two paths reach one state, DP is the right tool
Enumerate when only one solution is needed, paying exponential cost for no extra correctness

patterns.title: Choosing a Sort
patterns.summary: Every comparison sort costs at least n log n, so the choice is about constants, space, stability and adaptivity -- not about beating the bound. Beating it requires leaving the comparison model.
trigger_cues: Keys are integers in a small range, where counting or radix sort applies
Stability matters because equal keys carry different payloads
Worst-case guarantees are required, ruling out plain quicksort
Extra space is unavailable, ruling out mergesort
invariant_rules: Merge sort: both halves are sorted on entry, so emitting the smaller front element preserves order
Quicksort: after partitioning, every element at or before the pivot is at most the pivot
Counting sort: the prefix sum gives the exact count of keys below each key, so placement is arithmetic
A comparison sort needs n! distinct leaves, which is why n log n is a floor and not a target
common_pitfalls: Reaching for quicksort's expected behaviour without randomising the pivot, so sorted input degrades it to n squared
Using counting sort when the key range dwarfs the element count
Ignoring stability when equal keys carry differing metadata
Assuming the asymptotically optimal sort is the fastest -- heapsort has the worst memory pattern of any

patterns.title: Disjoint-Set Union for Connectivity
patterns.summary: Near-constant connectivity queries under merge-only workloads. The technique is only valid offline, and the two optimisations are not optional.
trigger_cues: Repeatedly merging groups and asking whether two elements are connected
Minimum spanning trees, redundant connection detection, connected components
The operations only ever merge; nothing is ever split
Queries are known in advance so results may be deferred to the end
invariant_rules: parent[x] == parent[y] if and only if x and y are in the same component
A union links only two distinct roots, so exactly two components merge
Path compression rewrites pointers within a tree and never moves an element between components
Union by rank keeps tree height at log n, since a depth increase implies a component at least doubled
common_pitfalls: Using it when edges are removed, which the merge-only restriction forbids; rollback union-find or a different structure is required
Omitting one of the two optimisations, which loses the alpha(n) bound and settles for O(log n)
Calling find for the answer without checking that the two elements are already connected before adding an edge
Assuming alpha(n) is O(1) as a formal claim; it is merely below 5 for any n that fits in memory

patterns.title: Bit Manipulation and XOR Decomposition
patterns.summary: Treat the word as independent bit positions. Every operation is O(1) on a fixed width, so nothing here improves a complexity class -- only constants, by up to the word size.
trigger_cues: A value occurs an even number of times except one, and it must be found
Parity, single-set-bit extraction, or power-of-two tests
A bounded index domain where a bitset beats a hash set
A range XOR or XOR-prefix query is needed
invariant_rules: x XOR x is zero and x XOR 0 is x, so even-multiplicity groups cancel and odd ones collapse to a copy
x AND (x - 1) clears exactly the lowest set bit, and is non-zero exactly when x is non-zero
Each mask operation affects exactly the positions its mask selects, because OR with 0, AND with 1 and XOR with 1 are all identity elsewhere
Signed shifts and 1 << 31 are undefined behaviour, so every bit routine takes unsigned
common_pitfalls: Applying 'XOR everything' when the precondition does not hold, producing a plausible number rather than an error
Using signed types, where a left shift into the sign bit is undefined rather than merely implementation-defined
Expecting a bit trick to make an exponential problem polynomial -- it cannot, because the operation count is unchanged
Treating a compound assignment as atomic under concurrency; it is a read-modify-write and loses updates

decision_matrix.scenario: Frequent random access and key-based lookup

candidates.space_overhead: High (buckets, hashes, and linked collision nodes)
candidates.best_when: Unordered key lookup where average O(1) performance is required
candidates.avoid_when: Sorted order iteration or strict worst-case latency bounds are mandatory

candidates.best_when: Keys must stay ordered, or predecessor/successor range queries are needed
candidates.avoid_when: Only raw equality lookups are needed and average O(1) is preferred

candidates.best_when: Dataset is immutable or bulk-loaded once and queried heavily
candidates.avoid_when: Frequent runtime insertions and deletions occur

decision_matrix.scenario: Continuous retrieval and streaming updates of minimum or maximum element

candidates.time_complexity: O(1) find extremum, O(log N) push/pop
candidates.best_when: Only need top priority element (min or max) without searching arbitrary keys
candidates.avoid_when: Need to search, delete, or update arbitrary middle elements

candidates.time_complexity: O(log N) min/max, O(log N) push/pop
candidates.best_when: Need extremum access AND arbitrary deletions / range lookups simultaneously
candidates.avoid_when: Only priority access is needed (unnecessary overhead)

candidates.best_when: Extremum is queried extremely rarely compared to writes
candidates.avoid_when: Streaming queries or frequent top-element consumption

decision_matrix.scenario: Frequent insertions and removals at the front or middle

candidates.time_complexity: O(1) insert/remove given node pointer, O(N) to seek by index
candidates.best_when: LRU caches, constant-time splice and node relocation with existing iterators
candidates.avoid_when: Need random access by index (O(N) traversal penalty)

candidates.time_complexity: O(1) push/pop at both front and back, O(1) indexed lookup
candidates.best_when: Sliding window buffers, job queues, double-ended queues
candidates.avoid_when: Frequent insertions in the middle of the collection

candidates.time_complexity: O(N) insert/remove at front/middle, O(1) amortized append
candidates.best_when: Appends and random index access dominate over prepends
candidates.avoid_when: Prepend or frequent middle deletions (requires shifting elements)

decision_matrix.scenario: Range queries [L, R], predecessor, successor, and sorted traversal

candidates.time_complexity: O(log N + K) range scan, O(log N) insert/delete
candidates.best_when: Dynamic dataset with real-time modifications requiring sorted bounds
candidates.avoid_when: Data is completely static or known upfront

candidates.time_complexity: O(log N + K) range scan, O(N) insert/delete
candidates.best_when: Static or read-only datasets with excellent CPU cache locality

candidates.time_complexity: O(N) full table scan for any range query
candidates.avoid_when: Any range query or sorted iteration is required
